content.title: Intersectionality as a framework for innovation in energy
content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations

content.text:
Innovation in energy systems must be not only technologically advanced but also socially inclusive.

This lesson explores how intersectionality—the interconnected nature of social categorizations such as gender, class, ethnicity, and geography—can serve as a transformative lens for fostering equitable and effective energy innovation.

Intersectionality, when treated as a design principle rather than a policy add-on, opens pathways for energy systems that are not only inclusive but epistemically plural—drawing on diverse worldviews, knowledge systems, and innovation cultures.

Recent empirical work has shown that without such justice-oriented integration, innovation risks entrenching structural inequalities, especially in the Global South.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: Part 1: Intersectionality is a lever for energy innovation

content.text:
Energy innovation does not occur in a vacuum—it is shaped by institutional legacies, governance frameworks, and the uneven distribution of power and resources.

 Intersectionality is a framework that examines how overlapping identities (gender, race, class, etc.) shape access to resources. This concept reveals how overlapping social identities mediate access to services and participation in energy systems. This approach is not merely theoretical: it redefines innovation as a justice-oriented process that responds to lived realities.

A 2024 study demonstrated that funding for energy innovation only leads to equitable outcomes when mediated by just transition principles—particularly around redistribution, participatory governance, and cultural recognition (Hosan et al., 2024).

In fact, empirical evidence shows that just transition mechanisms mediate 48–60% of the impact of energy funding on equity outcomes (Hosan et al., 2024). Innovation systems that ignore justice dimensions risk reinforcing exclusionary patterns, as seen in infrastructure-led approaches that failed to deliver real benefits to women and marginalized communities in Brazil and Colombia (Tomei et al., 2020; Leduchowicz-Municio et al., 2023).

The Brazilian experience from the Luz para Todos program provides an important example. As previously mentioned in module 2, Luz para todo is a Brazilian government program launched in 2003 to expand electricity access particularly in rural areas. Several lessons about intersectionality can be learned from this initiative:

content.body: Sespite its impressive reach—benefiting over 16 million people and installing more than 24,000 solar home systems—the program initially lacked a gender lens.

A 2023 gender impact assessment across 19 rural communities in Bahia showed that 100% of women were responsible for household chores, yet the energy systems installed (limited to 13 kWh/month) could not support appliances like washing machines or electric irons.
These capacity constraints perpetuated time poverty and limited productive use of energy by women.

content.text: Moreover, affordability mechanisms such as the Bolsa Família and TSE (tarifa social de energia) were more effective when targeted toward women, demonstrating how well-designed financial tools can improve gender equity in energy access (Leduchowicz-Municio et al., 2023).

Applying intersectionality to project evaluation reveals how benefits and burdens are distributed within communities. Ignoring local gender norms and spatial hierarchies can undermine well-intended energy programs—even when aggregate access metrics improve.
Intersectionality also requires recognizing cultural norms that shape participation.

For instance, long-term orientation and collectivism promote inclusive innovation, whereas power distance and individualism undermine it (Ullah et al., 2022). Innovation programs that do not account for these cultural dynamics risk elite capture and symbolic inclusion.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: Part 2: Inclusive Energy Policies for Market Design

content.text: Equity is not an afterthought—it is the design brief. energy markets must be reconstructed from the margins inward.

Markets and regulatory systems often reflect path dependencies that privilege some users over others. Inclusive energy policy must explicitly account for the varied ways in which gender, class, ethnicity, and geography shape access and affordability.


Recent findings from Argentina’s efforts to expand public service access in informal settlements reveal that improving energy inclusion goes beyond infrastructure upgrades.

Success depended heavily on:

Households expressed willingness to pay, but irregular incomes and administrative invisibility led to disconnection and debt cycles (Secretaría de Integración Socio Urbana, 2021).

This underscores that meaningful inclusion in energy systems must also address institutional fragmentation and legal uncertainty—especially in areas where residents face compounded barriers of tenure informality, affordability gaps, and administrative invisibility. A one-size-fits-all policy approach fails to capture intra-neighborhood diversity and systemic vulnerability.


Gendered policy design also plays a transformative role.

 In Brazil’s Bahia region, social programs that integrated gender considerations improved both financial inclusion and women’s social agency (Leduchowicz-Municio et al., 2023). These cases show that policy inclusion must span from tariff design to participatory governance.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: Part 3: Intersectional Approaches to Energy Entrepreneurship

content.text:
Entrepreneurship can drive clean energy transitions, but women, youth, and marginalized groups often face systemic barriers to finance, capacity, and legitimacy. Intersectional entrepreneurship reframes these challenges as design problems.


Recent UNDP-supported initiatives illustrate how youth- and Indigenous-led innovation can reshape the energy landscape from the ground up.

content.body: In the Amazon, Indigenous youth are spearheading solar energy projects that align with traditional knowledge and local governance, fostering energy autonomy while preserving cultural identity (UNDP, 2024a).

In Colombia, young entrepreneurs are using second-life batteries and solar kits to electrify underserved communities, creating circular economy solutions that address both waste and energy poverty (UNDP, 2024b).

content.text: These cases exemplify how intersectional energy innovation—grounded in territorial knowledge, generational renewal, and environmental justice—can deliver transformative impacts beyond the reach of top-down models.

content.body: Initiatives from Eswatini and India show that tailored support—combining finance, mentorship, and culturally responsive products—enabled women-led ventures to improve energy access and livelihoods (SEI, 2025).

In Brazil, despite high LPG usage, firewood remains prevalent due to cost, especially among women, who express unmet needs for refrigeration and tools—revealing gendered priorities and gaps (Leduchowicz-Municio et al., 2023).

content.text:
Cross-country analyses confirm that NGO partnerships and CSR engagement—not traditional R&D—are stronger predictors of environmental innovation in developing contexts (Ullah et al., 2022).

This highlights the importance of social capital, trust, and collective agency.

Certain cultural values significantly affect a country’s innovation outcomes. Intersectional frameworks must integrate both formal (laws, subsidies) and informal (social norms, cultural hierarchies) structures to accurately assess innovation equity. Intersectional innovation efforts must account for cultural variation in how risk, power, and time are perceived. These influence whose voices are heard and how innovation diffuses socially.

Therefore, inclusive energy futures will be built by broadening the definition of who gets to innovate, and why.

content.title: Key Takeaways
content.intro: If you only have space to remember 3 things:

takeaways.title: Intersectionality is not an intellectual luxury—it is a survival strategy for innovation. It asks: who decides, who benefits, and who bears the burden? And it insists that the answers must change.

A just energy transition will not come from replication of past systems under a green banner. It will emerge from co-designing with those excluded, valuing plural knowledge systems, and making equity the foundation rather than the fringe. Green finance, innovation ecosystems, and governance must be aligned to recognize and redistribute power.
The future of energy innovation belongs to those who see complexity not as a constraint, but as a source of strength. Intersectionality gives us that vision—and the tools to act on it.
